**Result: the complaint needs decomposing before it can be fixed, and the first spend should be on definition + a fixed eval set, not on models.**

Written to [search-relevance-diagnosis.md](<SCRATCH>/9CoOI6d9/search-relevance-diagnosis.md).

**The diagnosis.** "Irrelevant" resolves into ~6 failure modes living at different pipeline stages — intent understanding, retrieval recall (analyzer/CJK tokenization, over-restrictive filters, embedding-only retrieval missing exact SKUs), ranking order, cutoff/presentation (good result at position 11, no snippet highlight), corpus gap, and measurement artifact. Each has a different fix and a different owner, and they are separated by cheap numbers, not opinion.

**The order I'd insist on.** Two branching questions first: is this a *regression* (matching a deploy → replay a fixed query set old-vs-new and bisect config; days not weeks), and *which segment* complains (a pooled average hides a broken tail behind a healthy head, so every metric gets reported per segment). Then: locate where the good document disappears at each stage boundary (`recall@100` → post-rerank top-10 → displayed top-10) → explain that boundary on 50 hand-inspected failures → one-variable ablation with a pre-declared kill criterion and latency/cost budget → UX polish last.

**Headline metric.** "Satisfying result in top 3" rate tracks complaint volume better than nDCG, with `recall@100` and `nDCG@10` as the diagnostic pair underneath it. Judgments pooled from the current system plus one cheap alternative; double-judge 20% and report agreement — if κ is low, the rubric is the defect, not the ranker.

**Two honest limits.** The workspace was empty — no system, logs, or judgments — so I measured nothing, and the document is labelled as a plan, not a finding. And the reflexive fix (add a reranker or vector DB) is the expensive path: it improves the queries that already work, adds p95 latency and per-query cost, destroys attribution, and still needs the same eval set to prove it helped.

The parent agent has the full summary. The four things that would change the plan: regression status, complaining segment, whether logs exist, and corpus size.
sent_messages:
Result: search relevance diagnostic — plan written to <SCRATCH>/9CoOI6d9/search-relevance-diagnosis.md (workspace was empty; no code, logs, or judgments were provided, so nothing could be measured — the doc is a diagnostic structure + plan, explicitly labelled as not-a-finding).

Core argument (lead with this):
1. "Feels irrelevant" is a symptom covering ~6 distinct failure modes at different pipeline stages — intent/query understanding, retrieval recall (index, analyzer, CJK tokenization, over-restrictive filters, embedding-only missing exact SKUs), ranking order, cutoff/presentation (good doc at position 11, no snippet highlight, near-duplicate crowding), corpus gap, and measurement artifact (users wanted something the query never expressed). Each has a different fix and owner.
2. Therefore the first deliverable is not a fix list but (a) a definition of relevance with a graded rubric and (b) a fixed eval set — then stage-level numbers pick the fix.
3. Two branching questions come before everything: is this a regression (matches a deploy/reindex → replay a fixed query set old-vs-new and bisect config; days not weeks), and which segment carries the complaints (one language/tenant/vertical/query-length band — pooled averages hide a broken tail behind a healthy head; report all metrics per segment).
4. Diagnostic sequence with gates, mirroring tracing→profiling→ablation: Stage 0 regression check → Stage 1 locate the loss (recall@100 at each stage boundary, post-rerank top-10, displayed top-10) → Stage 2 explain the dominant boundary on 50 hand-inspected failures → Stage 3 one-variable ablation with pre-declared kill criteria + latency/cost budget → Stage 4 UX polish last.
5. Metrics: recall@100 (retrieval), nDCG@10/MRR (ranking), and a headline "satisfying result in top 3" rate that tracks complaint volume better than nDCG; online: CTR@1, reformulation rate, zero-result rate, abandonment. Judgments: pooled top-10 of current + one cheap alternative, 3-point scale, double-judge ~20%, report Cohen's κ (rule of thumb ~0.6) — if agreement is low, the rubric is the problem, not the ranker.
6. Timeline: ~4 days to definition + baseline (~200 judged queries), week 2 boundary analysis, weeks 2–3 failure shapes, week 3–4 one ablation. All effort figures are estimates, contingent on logs existing and judging capacity.
7. Explicitly argue against the common shortcut: adding an LLM reranker / vector DB first optimizes already-fine queries, adds p95 latency and per-query cost, and destroys attribution — and still needs the same eval set to prove it helped.

Caveat for the parent: no measurement was possible in this environment; if the parent has the actual system/logs, stages 0–1 are the parts to execute first and they are cheap.

Open questions that would change the plan: regression vs steady state; complaining segment; log availability/retention; corpus size and update rate; existing labeled eval set and judging capacity.
